official_sources.excerpt: > Replay past executions and fork to explore alternative paths in LangGraph LangGraph supports time travel through [checkpoints](/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers#checkpoints): * **[Replay](#replay)**: Retry from a prior checkpoint. * **[Fork](#fork)**: Branch from a prior checkpoint with modified state to explore an alternative path. Both work by resuming from a prior checkpoint. Nodes before the checkpoint are not re-executed (results are already saved). Nodes after the checkpoint re-execute, including any LLM calls, API requests, and [interrupts](/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) (which may produce different results). ## Replay Invoke the graph with a prior checkpoint's config to replay from that point. Replay re-executes nodes—it doesn't just read from cache. LLM calls, API requests, and [interrupts](/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) fire again and may return different results. Replaying from the final checkpoint (no `next` nodes) is a no-op. Use [`get_state_history`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graphs/#langgraph.graph.state.CompiledStateGraph.get_state_history) to find the checkpoint you want to replay from, then call [`invoke`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graphs/#langgraph.graph.state.CompiledStateGraph.invoke) with that checkpoint's config: from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver from typing_extensions import TypedDict, NotRequired from langchain_core.utils.uuid import uuid7 checkpointer = InMemorySaver() .compile(checkpointer=checkpointer) # Step 2: Find a checkpoint to replay from print(f"next={state.next}, checkpoint_id={state.config['configurable']['checkpoint_id']}") # Step 3: Replay from a specific checkpoint # Find the checkpoint before write_joke replay_result = graph.invoke(None, before_joke.config) ## Fork Fork creates a new branch from a past checkpoint with modified state. Call [`update_state`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graphs/#langgraph.graph.state.CompiledStateGraph.update_state) on a prior checkpoint to create the fork, then [`invoke`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graphs/#langgraph.graph.state.CompiledStateGraph.invoke) with `None` to continue execution. `update_state` does **not** roll back a thread. It creates a new checkpoint that branches from the specified point. The original execution history remains intact. # Find checkpoint before write_joke # Fork: update state to change the topic fork_config = graph.update_state( # Resume from the fork — write_joke re-executes with the new topic fork_result = graph.invoke(None, fork_config) print(fork_result["joke"]) # A joke about chickens, not socks When you call [`update_state`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graphs/#langgraph.graph.state.CompiledStateGraph.update_state), values are applied using the specified node's writers (including [reducers](/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#reducers)). The checkpoint records that node as having produced the update, and execution resumes from that node's successors.

# LLM Playground
Test and iterate on your prompts directly in the Langfuse Prompt Playground. Tweak the prompt and model parameters to see how different models respond to these input changes. This allows you to quickly iterate on your prompts and optimize them for the best results in your LLM app without having to switch between tools or use any code.
![LLM Playground](/images/docs/playground-overview.png)
Compare multiple prompt variants alongside each other. Execute them all at once or focus on a single variant. Each variant keeps its own LLM settings, variables, tool definitions, and placeholders so you can immediately see the impact of every change.
### Open your prompt in the playground
You can open a prompt you created with [Langfuse Prompt Management](/docs/prompt-management/get-started) in the playground.
### Open a generation in the playground
You can open a generation from [Langfuse Observability](/docs/observability) in the playground by clicking the `Open in Playground` button in the generation details page.
### Tool calling and structured outputs
The Langfuse Playground supports tool calling and structured output schemas, enabling you to define, test, and validate LLM executions that rely on tool calls and enforce specific response formats.
  Currently, Langfuse supports opening tool-type observations in the playground
**Tool Calling**
- Define custom tools with JSON schema definitions
- Test prompts relying on tools in real-time by mocking tool responses
- Save tool definitions to your project
- Jump into the playground from your OpenAI generation using structured output
You can add prompt variables in the playground to simulate different inputs to your prompt.
  ![Add prompt variables](/images/docs/playground-variables.png)
### Use your favorite model
You can use your favorite model by adding the API key for the model you want to use in the Langfuse project settings. Learn how to [set up an LLM connection](/docs/administration/llm-connection).
  ![Select the model you want to
  use](/images/docs/playground-model-selection.png)
Optionally, many LLM providers allow for additional parameters when invoking a model. You can pass these parameters in the playground when toggling "Additional Options" in the model selection dropdown. [Read this documentation about additional provider options](/docs/administration/llm-connection#advanced-configurations) for more information.
- For structured regression testing of prompt and model variants on datasets, use [Experiments](/docs/evaluation/core-concepts#experiments).

Every page is available as Markdown by appending `.md` to its URL, or by sending an `Accept: text/markdown` header. This page: `https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/playground.md`.

# Checkpointing
> Track, rewind, and summarize Claude's edits and conversation to manage session state.
Claude Code automatically tracks Claude's file edits as you work, allowing you to quickly undo changes and rewind to previous states if anything gets off track.
## How checkpoints work
As you work with Claude, checkpointing automatically captures the state of your code before each prompt you send that starts a turn.
Claude Code tracks all changes made by its file editing tools:
* Every prompt you send that starts a turn creates a new checkpoint
* Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session. Discarding an older checkpoint deletes the snapshot files that no remaining checkpoint references, except each file's first snapshot, which the VS Code extension uses as the baseline for its session diffs.
* Claude Code saves checkpoints with the conversation, so you can still run `/rewind` after you resume a session
* Claude Code deletes a session's file snapshots in the [retention sweep](/docs/en/claude-directory#cleaned-up-automatically), by default about 30 days after the session last saved one. Rewinding to a checkpoint whose snapshots are gone can fail with [`No files were restored`](/docs/en/errors#no-files-were-restored). To keep snapshots longer, set [`cleanupPeriodDays`](/docs/en/settings-reference#cleanupperioddays).
### Rewind and summarize
Run `/rewind`, or press `Esc` twice when the prompt input is empty, to open the rewind menu.
  If the prompt input contains text, double `Esc` clears it instead of opening the menu. The cleared text is saved to your input history, so press `Up` to recall it after you finish in the rewind menu.
The rewind menu lists the prompts you sent during the session. Select the point you want to act on, then choose an action:
* **Restore code and conversation**: revert both code and conversation to that point
* **Restore conversation**: rewind to that message while keeping current code
* **Restore code**: revert file changes while keeping the conversation
* **Summarize from here**: compress the conversation from this point forward into a summary, freeing context window space
* **Summarize up to here**: compress the conversation before this point into a summary, keeping later messages intact
The two code restore options appear only when the selected checkpoint has tracked file changes to revert. If no file edits were captured after that point, the menu offers only **Restore conversation**, the summarize options, and **Never mind**.
After restoring the conversation or choosing Summarize from here, the original prompt from the selected message is restored into the input field so you can re-send or edit it.
Choosing Summarize up to here leaves you at the end of the conversation with the input empty. With either summarize option, a **Summarized conversation** marker appears in the conversation where the compressed messages were.
#### Rewind past a cleared conversation
If you ran `/clear` earlier in the same Claude Code process, the rewind menu shows an additional entry at the top of the list labeled `/resume <session-id> (previous session)`. Select it to resume the conversation that was active before `/clear` ran. The entry is available until you exit Claude Code or resume a different session.
Summarizing doesn't change files on disk, and the original messages stay in the session transcript, so Claude can still reference the details. To guide what the summary focuses on, highlight a **Summarize** option with the arrow keys and type instructions where the row reads **add context (optional)**, then press `Enter`. Selecting the option with its number key summarizes immediately without instructions.
  Summarize keeps you in the same session and compresses context, like a targeted `/compact`. To branch off and try a different approach while preserving the original session intact, use [`/branch`](/docs/en/sessions#branch-a-session) or `claude --continue --fork-session` instead.
Checkpoints are particularly useful when:
* **Freeing context space**: summarize a verbose debugging session from the midpoint forward, keeping your initial instructions intact
### Bash command changes not tracked
Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands. For example, if Claude Code runs:
```bash theme={null}
These file modifications cannot be undone through rewind. Only direct file edits made through Claude's file editing tools are tracked.

official_sources.excerpt:
> No receipt, no trust.
As agents move from single replies to tool use, memory, delegation, and multi-step workflows, final-answer evaluation is no longer enough. SACP makes the intermediate work auditable: what was claimed, what evidence supports it, who owns the next step, whether memory was promoted safely, and where human approval is required.
It does not replace LangGraph, MCP, A2A, OpenClaw, or agent SDKs. It adds a small audit layer:
When an agent says "done", it should produce a checkable work receipt.
AgentOps Doctor is the first reference tool in this repo. Paste in messy agent output, and it returns a status code, claim findings, missing evidence, next owner, required fix, and a translated SACP receipt.
- a model claims tests passed without showing command output;
- a tool result is summarized without preserving evidence;
SACP turns these failures into auditable work records. The protocol is intentionally small: Markdown/YAML packets, local validators, dirty-run cases, and example receipts that can be inspected by humans and tools.
    A[Agent claim: done] --> B{Evidence attached?}
    B -- No --> C[Missing evidence]
    E -- No --> G[Derive receipt]
SACP does not decide whether the underlying task is true by itself. It makes the claim, evidence, approval boundary, current status, and next owner visible enough for a human or trusted system to check.
## Why OpenAI Models And Codex Matter
SACP is model-agnostic, but OpenAI models and Codex are a natural testbed because coding agents already perform long-horizon work: reading files, editing code, running tests, delegating subtasks, and reporting completion. API credits would be used to turn this repo into a stronger open-source evaluation harness:
- run GPT-based agent workflows and translate them into SACP receipts;
- test failure modes such as memory drift, delegated task drift, missing evidence, and tool-use audit gaps;
- compare baseline agent outputs against SACP-instrumented workflows;

receipt_completeness

Receipt Chain is an optional SACP profile for long-running work, multi-module work, multi-agent handoff, and cross-model continuation. It does not schedule agents. It preserves auditable work state between them.

community_issues.title: Long tool calls (~180s+) silently re-executed from checkpoint on LangGraph Cloud
community_issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem

When a tool call takes longer than ~3 minutes on LangGraph Cloud, it gets silently re-dispatched from the last checkpoint while the original is still running. Both the original and the duplicate complete successfully, resulting in 2-3x redundant work and cost.

We're using deepagents' `SubAgentMiddleware`, where the main agent dispatches sub-agents via a `task()` tool that internally calls `subagent.ainvoke()`. These sub-agents are standard LangGraph agents making multiple sequential LLM + tool calls, and they routinely take 3-10 minutes.

### What we observe

At ~180s after a long tool call starts, duplicate runs appear in the trace with:
- Identical tool call arguments (same content hash)
- Their own `tools` node but **no preceding `model` node** — so they're not triggered by an LLM decision
- Both original and duplicate complete successfully
- The pattern is consistent across langgraph 1.1.3 through 1.1.6, EU Cloud, Plus tier

### What we tried (no effect)

| Setting | Result |
|---------|--------|
| `BG_JOB_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS=900` | Still re-executes at ~180s |
| `BG_JOB_ISOLATED_LOOPS=true` | No change |
| `asyncio.to_thread()` wrapping the long call | Interval doubled to ~360s but still re-executes |

### What we found in the source

We looked at the installed `langgraph-api` (v0.7.28 and v0.7.96) to understand the mechanism:

- `BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT = 120` is hardcoded in `config/__init__.py` (not configurable via env var)
- The queue sweep runs every `BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT * 2` (240s) and calls `Runs.Sweep()` on the Go persistence server
- `Runs.enter()` opens a gRPC stream that "starts heartbeat and Redis cancellation listening on the server"
- The `listen_for_signals` task runs as a parallel `asyncio.Task`, so the gRPC stream should remain open during a long `await ainvoke()`
- `CancelledError` is explicitly retriable (`ALL_RETRIABLE_EXCEPTIONS`), so swept runs go back to `pending` and get re-dispatched

We also noticed that the Helm chart sets `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` while `BG_JOB_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS` defaults to 180s — but we're not sure if this applies to managed Cloud.

### What we don't understand

We can't inspect the Go server, so we don't know what criteria `Runs.Sweep()` uses to mark a run as stale. The gRPC stream from `Runs.enter()` appears to stay open (the listener task is async and should run concurrently), yet the run still gets swept.

Could you help us understand:

1. What does the Go server consider a "stale" run? Is it based on the gRPC stream health, a timer, checkpoint activity, or something else?
2. Is there anything we can do from the Python side to signal liveness during a long `await` inside a tool call?
3. Is `BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT` related to the stale detection, or is it only used for th

### Problem Statement

During long agentic sessions, Claude Code's context compaction triggers silently and drops information unpredictably. 

I was implementing a Logs tab feature for my embedded toolkit - JSON endpoint, parsing, display, filtering. Mid-task, compaction happened. The agent delivered a working feature - impressive given what it retained - but the filtering functionality got lost.

The problem: I had zero visibility into what was about to be dropped, and no opportunity to say "filtering is the critical part, prioritize that." The agent performed perfectly within its constraints, but I only discovered the gap when the task was "done."

- Log tab basic implementation ✓
- JSON endpoint structure ✓

Likely to lose detail on:
- Filtering feature
- Auto-refresh polling

community_issues.title: feat(in-app-agent): unbounded conversation context growth — no token-budget handling on replay
community_issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem

The in-app agent's conversation context grows without bound. Conversation history is event-sourced in `in_app_agent_events` and replayed into model messages on every step, and as far as I can tell there is no token-limit handling anywhere on that path — no truncation, no rolling window, no summarization:

- Replay: `getConversationMessagesForReplay` → `sanitizeConversationMessagesForReplay` in `packages/shared/src/in-app-agent/server/persistence.ts` only drops reasoning messages, redirect tool results, and unpaired tool calls — a syntax-level cleanup, not a budget.
- The only length-related mechanisms I found are storage-side (`compactPersistedEventDeltas` in `eventCompaction.ts` merges text/reasoning deltas) and the opt-in "silent MCP output" convention (`redactSilentToolMessages`, full results persisted to `/workspace/tool_calls` in the sandbox), which depends on the model choosing to pass `silent`.

So a long-running conversation eventually exceeds the model's context window and the run fails, with no graceful degradation.

### Proposed direction

A token-budget layer when building replay messages:

1. Estimate the replay payload against a configurable budget (tunable alongside the existing `IN_APP_AGENT_*` tunables).
2. When over budget, replace the oldest tool-result blocks with a short reference to the already-persisted full output (the `/workspace/tool_calls` convention already gives the agent a way to re-read them via the sandbox), or with a summary placeholder event.
3. Only trim from the tail of the history so the cache-stable prefix (system prompt compiled per run, volatile context appended as a trailing user message by `TrailingContextProcessor`) is preserved — mirroring the existing prompt-cache design.
4. Keep the three projections consistent: compaction happens at replay derivation, so `in_app_agent_events` stays the lossless source of truth and the display projection is unaffected.

### Scope / questions

- MVP could be tool-result-redaction only (no LLM summarization), which is deterministic and cheap to reason about; summarization could be a second step behind a tunable.
- Is this already on your roadmap for the assistant, or would a PR along these lines be welcome? Happy to write this up in more detail or start with a design sketch — the constraint I'd want maintainer input on is whether compaction should live in `sanitizeConversationMessagesForReplay` (shared) or in the worker-side runtime where the model call happens.

community_issues.title: Per-test-case `repeat` option to control how many times individual tests run
community_issues.body_excerpt:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

When evaluating LLM outputs, I want to run negative test cases (e.g., assertions that check the model does NOT produce a certain output) multiple times to verify consistency — since a model might pass once by chance. For positive test cases, a single run is sufficient. Currently, `repeat` is only configurable globally via `evaluateOptions.repeat`, which forces all test cases to run the same number of times. This means I either over-run positive tests (wasting cost/time) or under-run negative tests (risking false confidence).

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Allow `repeat` to be set at the individual test case level via the `options` field, for example:

```yaml
tests:
  - description: "Should tell a joke"
    assert:
      - type: contains
        value: "laugh"
    options:
      repeat: 1  # positive test, once is enough

  - description: "Should not hallucinate"
    assert:
      - type: not-contains
        value: "I don't know"
    options:
      repeat: 5  # negative test, run multiple times to verify consistency
```

When `options.repeat` is set on a test case, it should override the global `evaluateOptions.repeat` for that specific test case only.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- **Manually duplicating test cases in YAML:** Verbose and hard to maintain. Duplicated entries also make results harder to read in the output table.
- **Using `evaluateOptions.repeat` globally:** Forces all tests to run the same number of times, which wastes API calls and cost for positive test cases that don't need repeated sampling.

**Additional context**

This is especially useful for:
- **Consistency/flakiness testing:** Negative assertions (e.g., `not-contains`, `not-icontains`, `javascript` guards) benefit from multiple runs to catch non-deterministic failures.
- **Cost control:** Positive sanity-check tests don't need to be repeated, so per-test `repeat` avoids unnecessary API calls.

The change would likely be small — the `TestCaseSchema` in `src/types/index.ts` would need a `repeat` field added to the `options` object, and `src/evaluator.ts` (around line 2270) would need to prefer `testCase.options.repeat` over the global `options.repeat` when present.

community_issues.title: [Feature Request] Native auto-retry configuration for Google AI provider (Gemini) due to frequent 503/Overloaded errors
community_issues.body_excerpt:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Yes, I am experiencing frequent instability when using the Google AI (Gemini) provider. The API often fails with transient errors, which causes test suites to flake significantly.

Common errors include:
1. `Error: No output found in response: {"content":{},"finishReason":"STOP","index":0}`
2. `Error: No candidates returned in API response.`
3. `Got response: {"error":{"code":503,"message":"The model is overloaded. Please try again later.","status":"UNAVAILABLE"}}`

This is particularly problematic when these errors occur inside **LLMRubrics (graders)**. Instead of throwing an error that might trigger a global retry or simply mark the test as an error, the grader often fails to evaluate, resulting in a `FAIL` status (score 0) rather than an `ERROR`. This significantly skews the evaluation results/statistics, making the prompt look worse than it is due to API instability.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like to have a provider-specific configuration option for Google AI to enable auto-retries for specific transient errors (like 503 or empty responses).

Ideally, I could configure it in `promptfooconfig.yaml` like this:

```yaml
providers:
  - id: "google:gemini-3-pro-preview"
    config:
      maxRetries: 3 # or 'retry: 3'
      retryDelay: 1000 # optional
```

If the API returns a 503 Overloaded status or an empty candidate list, the provider should automatically retry the request `N` times before returning a final error to the promptfoo core.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I considered using the global CLI flag `--retry-errors` (or `retryErrors` config), but this is not ideal for my use case because:

1.  **Rubric Failures:** As mentioned, when an LLM grader fails due to these API glitches, it sometimes results in a failing grade (affecting the score) rather than a thrown Error that the global retry mechanism catches.
2.  **Granularity:** I specifically want to target the unstable Google provider without forcing retries on every other part of the system or other providers.
3.  **Data Injection:** My specific workflow for data injection makes using the global retry loop difficult/incompatible. I need the retry logic to happen at the provider execution level (encapsulated within the Google provider adapter).

**Additional context**
Google's Gemini API has been throwing `503 The model is overloaded` very frequently recently. Having a built-in backoff/retry mechanism specifically for this provider (similar to how some OpenAI client wrappers handle rate limits) would greatly improve the reliability of test runs in CI/CD pipelines.

community_issues.title: [agents] investigate clientside tracing for external tools
community_issues.body_excerpt:
## Context

Tracked under #11598.

When commit 71ceeb3fa6 ripped the v1 `/chat` route, we lost backend TOOL spans for tools that the AI SDK / browser executes (the pydantic-ai `ExternalToolset` tools: `bash`, `ask_user`, `set_time_range`, `read_prompt`, `edit_prompt`, `clone_prompt_instance`, `set_spans_filter`).

The new instrumentation in `OpenInferenceToolsetWrapper` only fires when pydantic-ai actually invokes `call_tool` server-side. `ExternalToolset.call_tool` raises `NotImplementedError` — pydantic-ai surfaces a `DeferredToolRequests` and the frontend executes the tool, so no backend `call_tool` ever happens for these tools.

## Short-term workaround (already landed)

`OpenInferenceAgentWrapper` backfills synthetic TOOL spans on the next turn by scanning the trailing `ToolReturnPart`s in the inbound `message_history` and emitting them as children of the AGENT span. This restores trace coverage but has structural problems:

- The TOOL span lives in turn N+1's trace, not the turn N trace where the model actually requested the tool.
- Span timestamps are synthetic (set at backfill time, not at actual tool execution time).
- We can't capture errors that happen client-side without piping more metadata back through the next request.

## Goal

Investigate emitting TOOL spans from the **client** at actual execution time, so:

- The TOOL span sits in the same trace as the LLM call that requested it.
- Span timing reflects real client-side execution duration.
- Client-side tool errors are captured natively.

Likely shape: extend the AI SDK tool-execution path on the frontend to start an OTel span around each external tool invocation, parented to the trace ID emitted in that turn's `message-metadata` chunk, and ship it to the same `/v1/traces` ingestion endpoint.

## Open questions

- How does the frontend currently get a tracer / OTel context? (We expose trace IDs via `AssistantMessageMetadata.trace`, but no tracer SDK is wired up yet.)
- Do we want tools to be timed end-to-end including UI-side approval prompts (e.g. `ask_user`), or just the execution portion?
- Schema: do client TOOL spans get emitted alongside server spans in the same trace, or as a sibling trace linked by `trace.id`?

## Done when

- A short design doc / spike result is captured here describing the chosen approach.
- A follow-up implementation issue is filed.
- The backfill workaround in `OpenInferenceAgentWrapper._emit_resolved_external_tool_spans` is removed.

community_issues.title: Docs safety guidance: auditable final-state receipts for agent completion claims?
community_issues.body_excerpt:
Hi, I maintain SACP, a small text-first receipt layer for AI agent work:
https://github.com/aDragon0707/sacp

I noticed LangGraph emphasizes durable execution, human-in-the-loop review, stateful agents, and long-running workflows. That seems like a natural place for guidance on auditable final-state receipts.

I also saw that this repo's `examples/` directory is archived and points users to the consolidated LangChain docs, so I am opening an issue instead of sending a docs PR to the wrong place.

Would LangGraph docs accept a small safety-oriented section or example about final completion receipts?

The pattern would document:

- what the agent claimed
- what evidence supports each claim
- who owns the next step
- whether human approval is required before publishing, deploying, writing memory, or taking another external action

Concrete failure mode:

```text
Done. All tests passed. Ready to publish.
```
